t: A Simple Exercise Program For Teachers
q: While it’s true that leaving home to exercise can be an initial motivator, eventually it becomes your biggest hurdle and a reason why more than 90% of people quit within three months.

But the truth is, fewer is harder because it never really becomes a habit. Exercising every day, on the other hand, is the easiest way to make it part of your lifestyle and eventually something you look forward to.
Interval training, on the other hand, which entails short bursts of exercise followed by rest, gives you more bang for your buck. Every study supports this.
The way to ensure you’re doing this is to give only 75% of your best effort.
Big results don’t come from big, dramatic changes—which are destined to fail. They come from small, quiet changes barely noticeable and repeated over time.
Before you know it, your daily workout will become a habit you can’t live without.
x: Recommends exercising at home to eliminate commute time, which he identifies as the biggest reason people quit within three months.
Advises exercising every single day rather than a few times a week, arguing daily repetition is what actually builds the habit.

t: How To Handle A Student Whose Grades (And Behavior) Have Dropped
q: The reason is that it prevents students from fighting through and overcoming trials and tribulations all on their own, which is infinitely more instructive.
When a student through grit and determination is able to rejoin the peloton of their own accord it makes them more resilient.
It extinguishes their intrinsic desire to improve and change their life circumstances—which is a trait the happiest, most successful people share and that many of our students are in short supply.

It’s important to note that if at any time you suspect bullying, trauma, homelessness, mental health issues, etc. or that they’re in a potentially dangerous situation, you must always and immediately step in.
It provides the tools we all need to survive, reverse course, and thrive in the end.

t: How To Handle Students Who Make Classmates Laugh
q: Should you hold all students who laugh accountable or just the student who started it?

Doing so is simply a matter of explaining that any behavior that attempts to make other students laugh during instructional time is a disruption and therefore transgresses rule #1 – Listen and follow directions.

The second key is to only enforce a consequence on the instigator, which attacks the misbehavior at its source and avoids the perceived unfairness of holding accountable those who, sometimes against their will, laughed.
It’s important to mention that when students repeatedly try to make others laugh, it’s a sign that you’ve been less than consistent in the past.
If your back is turned and you don’t know who misbehaved, then you’re out of luck.
With these two keys, plus your vigilance, this and other similar disruptions will rarely if ever happen again.
x: Advises enforcing consequences only on the instigator, not on students who merely laughed in response.

t: Is Your School Lying To You?
q: It says, “Your students can’t do it.” It tells them that the situation is hopeless, that their students are too far gone, so shaped and bent by bad influences that the good doesn’t stand a chance.
It’s a systemic failure that views a 1% improvement in abysmal reading scores as something to crow about.
You, after all, control the world within your classroom—at least, in a classroom management sense. Yes, it’s difficult when chaos runs roughshod over everything around you.
So move slower, speak deliberately and less frequently, and pause often. In between, teach and model every little detail you want your students to do or to know to the highest standard.

As such, you must require your students to prove to you they understand and have learned well the content of your lessons by doing, performing, or otherwise mirroring back to you what you’ve taught them.
If you invest the time to learn our approach, no school on earth can stop you from creating an oasis of truth and excellence in what may very well be a vast desert of dysfunction and disarray.
x: Identifies a demoralizing 'lie'—that certain students are too far gone—as originating from school culture, not the students themselves.
Linsin describes a demoralizing 'lie' whispered to teachers in the toughest schools: that their students are simply too far gone to reach.
Insists teachers retain full control within their own classroom regardless of the broader school's dysfunction.
Recommends slowing everything down and modeling even trivial routines to the highest standard as the first step to change.
Advises requiring students to prove they've learned material through demonstrable performance, not passive compliance.
